frames.narration: Before the move. The application writes to the old database. A snapshot was copied to the new database over about 7 hours, and the change stream, started at the snapshot position, has been applying every later write.
The stream delivers the change to the new database, which applies it in order. Applying twice would change nothing, so a restart is safe. The lag is under a second.

The verifier compares the two databases while they are live. Row counts match, and a checksum per range of 100,000 ids is the same on both sides for every range. It also compares a sample of real reads.
Cutover, first step. The router sends 5% of reads to the new database, then 50%, then all, watching errors and latency. Writes still go to the old database.

Second step. The lag is under the 2-second threshold, so the router freezes writes. Clients wait instead of failing. The stream drains its last entries in under a second, and the verifier confirms both sit at the same position.
The router points writes at the new database and unfreezes. The freeze lasted about 2 seconds. Sequences on the new database were set a million above the old maximum, so new ids cannot collide.

The stream now runs in reverse. Writes made on the new database are copied back into the old one, so it stays current. If the new system misbehaves, rollback is the same short freeze the other way, with no write lost. After the soak period the reverse stream is stopped and the old database is retired.
